variants.name: threading.Lock boundary + private _impl helpers
variants.idiom_name: public methods using with self._lock: + private _impl helpers
variants.implementation_notes: threading.Lock is not reentrant: a second acquire by the thread that holds it blocks, as the documentation states, so a component whose public methods call each other must keep re-acquisition out of its call graph. The realization is a public method that wraps its body in with self._lock: and a private helper family (find_impl, _find_locked) that assumes the lock is held and touches the state directly. The GIL makes built-in operations atomic but not compound updates, so the discipline is about invariant atomicity under thread switches and, on free-threaded builds, about genuine parallelism. RLock is the documented escape hatch when restructuring is impractical - it stops the deadlock at the price of owner/recursion bookkeeping and of hiding the double acquisition - and queue.Queue or a single-consumer design removes the need entirely when the state can be owned by one thread.
pitfalls: threading.Lock is not reentrant: acquiring it twice from the same thread deadlocks with no error message and an unhelpful traceback.

Private naming is a convention only; a helper called from another module silently mutates unguarded state, and free-threaded CPython builds turn that into a genuine race rather than a GIL-protected interleaving.
RLock fixes the nesting but not the design: it hides the extra acquisition, adds owner/recursion bookkeeping, and synchronous helpers still block callers.
Never hold the lock across blocking I/O on a hot component if other threads need it, and do not mix Lock and RLock guarding the same state.

variants.name: asyncio.Lock boundary in an async component
variants.idiom_name: public coroutines using async with lock + synchronous private helpers
variants.implementation_notes: For an asyncio component the lock is asyncio.Lock: it is not thread-safe, it has no owner and it is not reentrant - acquire waits until the lock is unlocked, which cannot happen while the holder is awaiting the same acquire - so the same discipline applies one level up: the public coroutine takes the lock with async with lock: and the internal helpers are plain synchronous functions that assume it is held. Because the lock only governs interleaving at await points, keep every await that touches the guarded state inside the single critical section, and prefer a single owning task (an actor-style loop over an asyncio.Queue) when the component's operations no longer compose into one atomic step.
pitfalls: The lock only guards interleaving: a coroutine that awaits inside the critical section is still inside it, and a helper that awaits another public method of the component deadlocks (asyncio.Lock is not reentrant and has no owner).
Mixing asyncio.Lock with threads is a bug - the asyncio primitives are not thread-safe; use asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe or a threading.Lock for cross-thread work.
asyncio.Lock takes no timeout argument; bound long waits with asyncio.wait_for, which raises TimeoutError while the acquire is pending.
